# DepthLab, English

DepthLab is a Tel Aviv studio for live visuals, projection mapping and interactive installations, from stage shows to permanent rooms.

Founder: Zori Baazov (Hebrew: זורי באזוב), VJ & Real-Time Experience Creator. He founded DepthLab in January 2024 and designs and runs live visuals for musicians, audiovisual shows, clubs and festivals.

- Live shows and audiovisual shows: Zori designs and runs live visuals for musicians and audiovisual shows across Israel. [Daskal](https://depth-lab.com/work/daskal-live-show/), a keyboardist, composer and producer, performs with a timecode show that Zori built for the set (a visual language for the set, content synced to the music via timecode, a cue list) and has run live at every date since 2025. For [Omri Smadar's party](https://depth-lab.com/work/audio-reactive-stage-mapping/) in September 2026, the studio designed the stage and made custom video mapping for it, together with Erez Cohen: an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log with real-time generative scenes; earlier, for Omri Smadar's live shows in December 2025, Zori made audio-reactive visuals for each song with a live closed-circuit camera. Other live work: club nights at [Oman 17](https://depth-lab.com/work/oman-17-club-nights/) in Tel Aviv in 2025, where Zori played live visuals as VJ, and [White Night 2025](https://depth-lab.com/work/white-night-tel-aviv-museum/) at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art, where he ran the visuals for three stages in parallel.
- Interactive work: content that responds to people, built with depth cameras, LiDAR and body tracking, in tools such as TouchDesigner, Unreal Engine and GLSL. At [Midburn 2025](https://depth-lab.com/work/midburn-led-cube/), the people around Zori's LED cube became part of the visuals at night. In development: an immersive rehabilitation room for a hospital's clinical team, with markerless body tracking on depth cameras.
- LED work: [a 2.5 m 3D LED tower](https://depth-lab.com/work/led-tower-live/) of four LED modules (about 20,400 pixels), mapped in 3D and played live by Zori from TouchDesigner over Art-Net in November 2026; [an LED DJ stage concept](https://depth-lab.com/work/led-dj-stage-concept/) simulated in Unreal Engine with every LED, the club lights and the music (not built yet); and [the Midburn 2025 LED cube](https://depth-lab.com/work/midburn-led-cube/), about 49,000 pixels, where a depth camera turned the people around it into light.
- Experiments: [LAB](https://depth-lab.com/work/lab-video-mapping/), where Zori runs his experiments before they reach the real world: LEDs that follow his hand, live closed-circuit cameras, real-time AI, generative visuals and video mapping on real objects such as a carved relief.

Live visuals, projection mapping and interactive installations
DepthLab is the Tel Aviv studio of VJ Zori Baazov: live visuals for musicians and audiovisual shows, projection mapping and interactive installations for venues, events and brands across Israel.

## Who the services are for

### Musicians and artists
DepthLab turns a live set into an audiovisual show, as in Daskal's timecode show, run live by Zori at every date, and Omri Smadar's live shows, with audio-reactive visuals and a live camera. For Omri Smadar's party, DepthLab designed the stage and made custom video mapping for it. The studio also creates interactive content that responds to the people in the room.
Related work: Daskal Live Show: Timecode Visuals (https://depth-lab.com/work/daskal-live-show/); Omri Smadar's Party: Stage Design and Video Mapping (https://depth-lab.com/work/audio-reactive-stage-mapping/)

### Event producers, clubs and festivals
Live visuals for club nights, festivals and events with several stages, from show design to live operation. Zori ran the visuals for three stages in parallel at White Night at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art, and played live visuals as VJ at club nights at Oman 17 in Tel Aviv.
Related work: Visuals for Three Stages at White Night, Tel Aviv Museum of Art (https://depth-lab.com/work/white-night-tel-aviv-museum/); VJ for Club Nights at Oman 17 (https://depth-lab.com/work/oman-17-club-nights/)

### Venues and permanent installations
Immersive projection rooms and permanent installations for entertainment venues, from site survey to handover. The three VIP rooms DepthLab designed at an entertainment venue run every day without an operator, and the venue staff choose what plays.
Related work: Immersive VIP Room Design (https://depth-lab.com/work/immersive-vip-rooms/)

### Museums, malls and brands
Interactive installations with depth cameras, LiDAR and body tracking, and real-time AI installations, starting with the AI mirror in R&D. At Midburn, the people around Zori's LED cube became part of the visuals at night.
Related work: LED Cube Installation at Midburn (https://depth-lab.com/work/midburn-led-cube/); Real-Time AI Mirror (https://depth-lab.com/work/real-time-ai-mirror/)

## Live Visuals & VJ
URL: https://depth-lab.com/live-show/

DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of VJ Zori Baazov, designs and runs live visuals and VJ for musicians, artists, event producers, clubs and festivals across Israel, from club nights to audiovisual shows. The work covers show design with the lighting designer and the production, content synced to the music via timecode, visuals that react to the sound, and live operation at every date. On stage, Zori mostly works with electronic music and wants the visuals to follow the arrangement of a set: the drops and the breakdowns.

- Show design with the lighting designer, the director and the production
- A visual language and video art made for the artist's set
- Content synced to the music via timecode, with a cue list
- Visuals that react to each song, with a live camera and real-time generative scenes
- Interactive content that responds to people, with depth cameras and LiDAR
- Live operation at every date, on LED screens or projection
- VJ sets for club nights, parties and fashion shows
- Visuals coordinated across several stages at one event

### Visuals for musicians
For each show, the studio builds a visual language for the set and plans how it follows the music. For Daskal, a keyboardist, composer and producer, the content is synced to the music via timecode with a cue list, and Zori Baazov runs the show live at every date. For Omri Smadar's live shows, the studio made visuals for each song that react to the audio, with a live closed-circuit camera. For Omri Smadar's party, it designed the stage and mapped video onto an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log.

### Club nights and festivals
At club nights, Zori plays live VJ sets, as at Oman 17 in Tel Aviv. At festivals and cultural events, the visuals can be planned across several stages. At White Night at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art, Zori ran the visuals for three stages in parallel: supplier coordination, content management, and coordinating the lighting artists and video artists across the stages.

### Experience and tools
Zori Baazov started as a VJ in clubs, at parties and fashion shows. Later he worked as a VJ and real-time operator on large concert productions: LED screens, projection, on-stage troubleshooting, and working with directors, lighting designers and artists. His tools include Resolume Arena, TouchDesigner, Smode, timecode and DMX / Art-Net / sACN.

1. Brief: We go through the music, the stage, the screens and the dates.
2. Show design: A visual language for the set, planned with the lighting designer and the production.
3. Content and timecode: Content is made for the stage and synced to the music, with a cue list for the show.
4. Live: Zori operates the visuals live at every date.

Q: Who does live visuals and VJ for concerts and club nights in Israel?
A: DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of VJ Zori Baazov, designs and runs live visuals and video art for concerts, club nights, parties and festivals across Israel. Work includes the timecode show for Daskal, club nights at Oman 17 in Tel Aviv and the visuals for three stages at White Night at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.

Q: Who can create interactive visual content for an audiovisual show in Israel?
A: DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of VJ Zori Baazov, creates and runs visuals for music shows across Israel and builds interactive installations that respond to people. The show visuals include content that changes with the sound and real-time generative scenes. For Omri Smadar's live shows, each song got its own audio-reactive visuals with a live closed-circuit camera, and for his party the studio designed the stage and mapped video onto an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log. At Midburn, the people around an LED cube that Zori built became part of the visuals at night. For a new piece that follows people's movement, the studio can plan depth cameras, LiDAR or body tracking. Zori's tools include TouchDesigner, Resolume Arena, Unreal Engine 5 and GLSL.

Q: What does a VJ do at a concert or a club night?
A: A VJ plays and mixes visuals live on the screens or the projection, in time with the music. At a concert, the VJ often runs a show built for the set; at a club night, the VJ plays the visuals through the night. At DepthLab, Zori Baazov mostly works with electronic music and wants the visuals to follow the arrangement of each set: its drops and breakdowns.

Q: What is a timecode show?
A: In a timecode show, the visuals are locked to the music by a shared time signal, so each cue lands at the same moment in the track at every show. The content is built for the set and organized in a cue list. In the Daskal live show, Zori also operates the visuals live at every date.

Q: What is the difference between a timecode show, a live VJ set and audio-reactive visuals?
A: In a timecode show, every cue is locked to the track, so each cue lands at the same moment in the music at every date, as in Daskal's live show. In a live VJ set, the VJ plays and mixes the visuals live during the night, as at the club nights at Oman 17 in Tel Aviv, where Zori played live visuals as VJ. The third mode reacts to the sound: the visuals change as the music plays, as in the visuals DepthLab made for each song of Omri Smadar's live shows. The three can be combined in one show.

Q: Can you build a visual show for an artist's live set and run it at every date?
A: Yes. For Daskal, a keyboardist, composer and producer, the studio built a visual language for the set, synced the content to the music via timecode and set up a cue list. Zori runs the show live at every date.

Q: Do you do visuals for fashion shows?
A: Yes. Zori Baazov started as a VJ in clubs, at parties and fashion shows, and VJ sets for fashion shows are part of DepthLab's live visuals service. Send the date, the venue and details of the screens or projection on site.

Q: What does a VJ need from the venue or the production?
A: A VJ usually needs screens or a projector, a video connection from the control desk to the screens, power, and time on site to set up and test before doors open. Send the technical rider, the stage plan, the screen sizes and resolutions, and the schedule. If there are no screens yet, the studio can plan LED screens or projection with suppliers.

Q: How much does a VJ or a live visual show cost in Israel?
A: DepthLab does not publish prices, because every show is different. The cost depends on the number of dates and stages, how much new content is needed, timecode programming, the screens or projectors, and the setup and rehearsal time. Send the details on Instagram or LinkedIn for a quote.

Q: Do you work outside Tel Aviv, and in which languages?
A: Yes. DepthLab is based in Tel Aviv and works across Israel, with projects in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, the Judean Desert and at Midburn in the Negev. Zori speaks Hebrew, English, Russian and Georgian.

## Projection Mapping & Multi-Projector Setups
URL: https://depth-lab.com/video-mapping/

DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, plans and runs projection mapping, also called video mapping, for venues, malls, brands, event producers, festivals, artists and museums across Israel. The work covers the whole chain: site survey, projector and lens planning, blending several projectors into one image, mapping the content to the real surface and calibration on site. Projects include three immersive VIP rooms at an entertainment venue, with five to six projectors per room, and a building facade at Hasifa Music Festival in Jerusalem.

- Site survey and measurement of the surface or room
- Projector and lens planning, with equipment through suppliers
- Blending several projectors into one continuous image
- Content mapped to the geometry and viewing position of the space
- Mapping on stage sets and objects for live shows
- Calibration on site
- Live operation from a control desk, or unattended playback

### What we map
Rooms: three VIP rooms at an entertainment venue, each with five to six projectors blended across three walls, about 270 degrees. Objects on stage: for Omri Smadar's party, the studio mapped video onto an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log. A building facade: at Hasifa Music Festival in Jerusalem, the mapping was run live from a control desk.

### Experience
Zori Baazov worked as a VJ and real-time operator on large concert productions, with LED screens and projection. Then he founded DepthLab, and since then he has worked directly with clients, taking projects from site survey to handover: specification, system design, suppliers and budget, content, installation and calibration.

1. Site survey: We visit the space, measure the surface and check the light, the power and where projectors can go.
2. Projector plan: Projectors and lenses are chosen for the image size and the throw distance.
3. Content: Content is made to the measured geometry, so it sits on the real surface.
4. Install and calibrate: The projectors go up, and the image is blended, mapped and calibrated on site.
5. Show or handover: The mapping runs live from a control desk, or plays on its own in a permanent setup.

Q: What is projection mapping (video mapping)?
A: Projection mapping, also called 3D projection mapping, is video made to fit the measured shape of a real surface, such as a room, a stage set, an object or a building facade. When one projector is not enough, several projectors are blended into one image. DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, plans the whole chain, from site survey to calibration on site.

Q: Who does projection mapping in Israel?
A: DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio founded by Zori Baazov, plans and runs projection mapping across Israel, from immersive rooms to stage pieces and a building facade. Projects include three VIP rooms at an entertainment venue, with five to six projectors per room, and facade mapping at Hasifa Music Festival in Jerusalem.

Q: What is the difference between video art and projection mapping?
A: Video art is the visual content itself, shown on screens or in a projection. Projection mapping fits that content to the shape of a real surface, such as a wall, a stage set or a building, so it sits on the surface exactly. DepthLab makes both: the content, and the mapping that fits it to the surface.

Q: Can you map video onto a stage set or objects?
A: Yes. For Omri Smadar's party, the studio designed the stage and mapped video onto an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log, with real-time generative scenes. Stage projection mapping starts with measuring the objects, so the content fits their real shape.

Q: Can you do projection mapping for a festival or a city event?
A: Yes. DepthLab mapped a building facade at Hasifa Music Festival in Jerusalem and ran it live from a control desk. A festival or city project starts with a site survey of the surface and the event's schedule, since the mapping can only run after dark.

Q: Does projection mapping work outdoors or in daylight?
A: Projection needs darkness. Outdoors, a mapping show works after sunset, and the more ambient light there is, the more projector brightness is needed. For daylight, LED screens are the usual choice.

Q: What is multi-projector blending?
A: Blending, or edge blending, joins the images of several projectors into one seamless picture: the edges overlap and fade into each other, so a large wall or a whole room reads as one image. In the VIP rooms DepthLab designed, five to six projectors per room cover three walls, about 270 degrees. How many projectors a surface needs depends on its size, the throw distance and the ambient light, which the site survey checks.

Q: Which software do you use for projection mapping?
A: The studio's tools include Resolume Arena, TouchDesigner, Smode and Unreal Engine 5, with timecode when the mapping follows music. The choice depends on the surface, the content, and whether the mapping runs live from a control desk or plays on its own.

Q: What does the venue need to provide for video mapping?
A: The venue needs to give access for a site survey, a safe place to mount the projectors at the right distance from the surface, power, and darkness during the show. To start, send photos, measurements or plans of the surface, and the dates. Projectors and lenses can come through suppliers as part of the plan.

Q: How long does it take to prepare a projection mapping project?
A: It depends on the surface and on how much new content is needed. Every project needs a site survey, a projector plan, and setup and calibration time on site; content made for the geometry adds production time. Send the date early so the plan can work back from it.

Q: How much does projection mapping cost?
A: DepthLab does not publish prices, because each project is different. The main cost factors are the size of the surface, the throw distance, the ambient light, the number of projectors, the length of the content and the number of setup and show days.

## LED Installations & LED Stages
URL: https://depth-lab.com/led/

Zori builds looks for LED pieces where every pixel has its place in 3D, from a 2.5 m LED tower he played live to a cube at Midburn that reacted to the people around it. The looks are prepared on a 3D model of the real LEDs, so shapes, colours and timing are set before the night, and then run live from his TouchDesigner deck over Art-Net. For stages that are not built yet, he designs the whole set in Unreal Engine: the LEDs, the club lights and the music together.

- Looks built for the real pixel map: 3D content that reads from every side of the piece
- A 3D model of every LED, to design and check the show before the build
- Live operation from TouchDesigner over Art-Net, with cues for the set
- Interactive LED pieces that respond to people, with depth cameras
- LED stage and DJ booth concepts in Unreal Engine, rendered with the club lights and the music

1. Brief: The space, the music and the LED hardware: module sizes, pixel counts and controllers.
2. Pixel map: Every module is placed in 3D the way it really stands, and test patterns check every row and pixel.
3. Looks: Content and cues are built on the 3D model and checked from the crowd's point of view.
4. Live: On the night the looks run on the real LEDs, operated live.

Q: Who makes content for LED installations and 3D LED in Israel?
A: DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of VJ Zori Baazov, builds looks for 3D LED pieces and runs them live from TouchDesigner, from a 2.5 m LED tower to an interactive LED cube at Midburn.

Q: Can I see an LED stage before it is built?
A: Yes. Zori models the stage and every LED in Unreal Engine, keys the club lights to the same music and renders the show, so the design and the content can be checked before anything is built. The LED DJ stage on this site exists only as such a simulation for now.

Q: Do you need to know the LED hardware in advance?
A: Yes: module sizes, pixel counts and controllers. The looks are built for the real pixel map, so on site the mapping is checked and the show runs as designed.

Q: Can the LEDs react to people or to the music?
A: Yes. With depth cameras the LEDs can respond to the people around them, as with the LED cube at Midburn, and looks can follow the music live.

## Permanent Installations & Immersive Rooms
URL: https://depth-lab.com/installations/

DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, designs and builds immersive projection rooms and permanent installations for entertainment venues, malls, museums and brands across Israel. An immersive room surrounds the viewer with projection on several walls. The studio takes each room from site survey to handover, and the finished system can run every day without an operator, as in the three VIP rooms it delivered at an entertainment venue.

- Site survey, specification and system design: projectors, LED, media servers and sensors
- Suppliers and budget
- Content made for each room's geometry and viewing position
- Installation, blending and calibration
- Automated playback that venue staff run without an operator
- Themed worlds for kids, teens and adults

### Who it is for
Immersive rooms suit entertainment venues, such as family entertainment centers, and malls, museums and brands that want a permanent immersive experience. In the VIP rooms DepthLab designed, more than a dozen themed worlds serve kids, teens and adults, and venue staff choose them without an operator. For the same kinds of spaces, the studio is also developing real-time AI installations, starting with an AI mirror that is still in R&D.

1. Site survey: We measure the room and the viewing positions, and check the light and the power.
2. Specification: Projectors, media server, suppliers and budget are planned and agreed.
3. Content: Worlds are made for the measured walls, for example in Unreal Engine with a camera rig matched to the room.
4. Install and calibrate: Projectors are installed, and the image is blended and calibrated in the room.
5. Handover: Playback is automated, and venue staff choose the content without an operator.

Q: What is an immersive room?
A: An immersive room is a space where projection covers several walls around the viewer, so the image surrounds the people in the room. In the VIP rooms DepthLab designed at an entertainment venue, each room wraps the viewer on three walls, about 270 degrees.

Q: What is the difference between an immersive room and an interactive room?
A: In an immersive room, projection covers several walls and surrounds the people inside, as in the three VIP rooms DepthLab delivered at an entertainment venue. In an interactive room, the content also responds to the people, through depth cameras, LiDAR or body tracking. The two can be combined in one space.

Q: Who builds immersive projection rooms in Israel?
A: DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio founded by Zori Baazov, designs and builds immersive projection rooms and permanent installations across Israel, from site survey to handover. It delivered three VIP rooms at an entertainment venue, with five to six projectors per room and sixteen visuals, which run every day without an operator.

Q: How many projectors does a three-wall room need?
A: It depends on the size of the room, the throw distance and how bright the image must be. In the VIP rooms DepthLab designed, each room uses five to six projectors to cover three walls, about 270 degrees. A site survey gives the real number for your room.

Q: Can two rooms be joined into one image?
A: Yes. In DepthLab's installation at an entertainment venue, two of the three VIP rooms can open into one continuous image.

Q: Can a permanent installation run without an operator?
A: Yes. In the VIP rooms DepthLab designed, seamless loops run daily in Resolume Arena as the permanent runtime. Venue staff choose the loops, and no operator is needed.

Q: Can one room have different worlds for kids, teens and adults?
A: Yes. The VIP rooms DepthLab designed have sixteen visuals, more than a dozen themed worlds for kids, teens and adults, including Jungle, Casino, Mansion, Sky City, Football, City Sunset and Hero City. Venue staff choose which world plays.

Q: What does a venue need to prepare for a site survey?
A: For a site survey, the venue gives access to the room and sends its measurements or plans, the places people will watch from, and details about the light and the power. The survey checks where projectors can go and how the image can reach every wall.

Q: How long does an immersive room project take?
A: It depends on the number of rooms and how much content is made. For reference, the three VIP rooms DepthLab designed, with sixteen visuals, were delivered within about four months.

Q: How much does an immersive projection room cost?
A: DepthLab does not publish prices. The cost depends on the size and number of rooms, the number of projectors, the media server, how many worlds are made, and the installation and calibration work.

## Interactive & Sensors
URL: https://depth-lab.com/interactive/

DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, builds interactive installations and interactive content for museums, malls, venues, events, music shows and parties across Israel. Depth cameras, LiDAR and markerless body tracking let the content respond to the people in front of it, with nothing to wear or hold. The studio plans the sensors, builds the real-time content in tools such as TouchDesigner, Unreal Engine and GLSL, then installs and tunes it on site. Work includes an LED cube at Midburn, where at night the people around it became part of the visuals, and a real-time AI mirror in R&D.

- Motion tracking with depth cameras and LiDAR
- Markerless body tracking: nothing to wear or hold
- Interactive projection, interactive walls and floors, and LED content that respond to movement
- Content for music shows, parties and festivals, where the people in the space become part of the visuals
- Real-time content and creative coding in TouchDesigner, Unreal Engine and GLSL
- Sensor setup, calibration and testing on site

1. Idea and space: We look at the space, the visitors or the audience, and what they should do in front of the piece.
2. Sensors: Depth cameras or LiDAR are chosen to detect movement and placed for the area that needs tracking.
3. Content and logic: The content and the way it responds are built and tested with people moving in front of it.
4. Install and tune: On site, the tracking and the content are tuned to the real light and space.

Q: Who makes interactive installations in Israel?
A: DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, builds interactive installations across Israel, with depth cameras, LiDAR and body tracking, so the content responds to people. Work includes an LED cube at Midburn, where at night the people around the cube became part of the visuals, and a real-time AI mirror in R&D.

Q: Can interactive content be part of a music show, a party or a festival?
A: Yes. At Midburn, the people around the LED cube that Zori built at home became part of the visuals at night. Content can also react to the music itself: for Omri Smadar's live shows, the studio made audio-reactive visuals for each song with a live closed-circuit camera. For a new piece, the studio can plan depth cameras or LiDAR that track where people are and how they move, so the visuals change with them in real time.

Q: Can you build an interactive wall or floor for a mall or a museum in Israel?
A: Yes. DepthLab plans the sensors, usually depth cameras or LiDAR, builds the real-time content in TouchDesigner, Unreal Engine or GLSL, then installs and tunes it on site, anywhere in Israel. The content can respond to steps, gestures or simply to people walking by, on a projected wall or floor or on LED screens.

Q: How does a projection that responds to movement work, with no sensors on the body?
A: A depth camera measures the distance to every point it sees, so the software can find people and follow their movement without suits, markers or wearables. That movement becomes data, and the content on the wall, the floor or the screen changes in real time. DepthLab is developing an immersive rehabilitation room with markerless body tracking on depth cameras, for a hospital's clinical team.

Q: What is a depth camera, and when is LiDAR used instead?
A: A depth camera measures how far each point in front of it is, so the software can separate people from the background and follow their bodies at close range. Many depth cameras use infrared light, so they also work in a dark projection space. LiDAR measures distance with laser light and is often used to detect presence or touch across a wall or a floor. DepthLab chooses the sensor by the size of the area and the light in the space.

Q: Can an interactive installation use AI?
A: Yes. In DepthLab's real-time AI mirror, the visitor's live camera image is the input: you stand in front of a camera and see yourself in another world. It runs locally on one GPU at about 10 FPS and is still in R&D.

Q: Can an interactive installation run all day without staff?
A: Yes, when it is planned as a permanent piece with automatic start-up and simple controls for the staff. The studio's permanent installation in three VIP rooms already runs daily with no operator: venue staff choose the content in Resolume Arena.

Q: What affects the cost of an interactive installation?
A: DepthLab does not publish prices. The main factors are the size of the area, the number of sensors, screens or projectors, how complex the interaction is, how much content is made, and whether it is for one event or permanent.

## Content, 3D & AI
URL: https://depth-lab.com/3d-ai/

DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, makes custom content for LED screens, projection mapping and immersive rooms, for venues, artists and musicians, event producers and brands across Israel. The work covers seamless loops, 3D animation and worlds in Unreal Engine 5 and Blender, real-time generative scenes and AI-generated content, produced on local and cloud pipelines. Each piece is made for the real screen or surface, at its resolution and geometry. For three VIP rooms at an entertainment venue, the studio made sixteen visuals, mostly in Unreal Engine, rendered as one wide canvas of 5120 x 800 px per room.

- Seamless loops made for your venue's screens or walls, ready to run daily on a media server
- 3D worlds and animation in Unreal Engine 5 and Blender, for projection and LED screens
- Scenes generated in real time for live shows and stage mapping
- AI-generated content on local and cloud pipelines
- Content adapted to the geometry and viewing position of each space

### Rendered in advance or generated live
Some content is rendered in advance and plays as seamless loops, like the sixteen visuals that run daily in the VIP rooms the studio designed. Other content is generated live while the show runs. For Omri Smadar's live shows, the studio made audio-reactive visuals for each song with a live closed-circuit camera, and for his party it mapped video onto an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log on stage, with real-time generative scenes.

1. Canvas: We start from the real screen or wall: resolution, shape and where people watch from.
2. Look: References and test frames set the look before full production.
3. Production: 3D, AI and motion work, rendered at the full size of the canvas or built to run in real time during a show.
4. Delivery: Rendered loops are encoded and tested on the media server; real-time scenes are set up and tested in the space.

Q: Who creates content for LED screens and projection in Israel?
A: DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, creates custom content for LED screens, projection mapping and immersive rooms across Israel, from seamless loops to 3D worlds and AI-generated content. For three VIP rooms at an entertainment venue, it made sixteen visuals, each adapted to the geometry and viewing position of its room.

Q: Who makes 3D animation for projection or LED screens in Israel?
A: DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, makes 3D animation and worlds in Unreal Engine 5 and Blender for projection, LED screens and immersive rooms. The worlds for the VIP rooms it designed were built mostly in Unreal Engine, with a camera rig matched to the measured walls, and rendered as one wide canvas per room.

Q: What resolution should content be for a wide multi-projector canvas?
A: The content is made at the size of the full canvas the projectors cover once they are blended. In the VIP rooms DepthLab designed, each room is one canvas of 5120 x 800 px across three walls. The exact size comes from the projector plan for your space.

Q: What is the difference between pre-rendered content and real-time generative visuals?
A: Pre-rendered content is made before the event and plays back as video, often as seamless loops on a media server. Real-time generative visuals are calculated by software while the show runs, so they can change with the music or the moment. DepthLab makes both: rendered loops for permanent rooms, and live scenes mapped onto objects on stage at Omri Smadar's party.

Q: Can AI-generated video be used on venue screens or in a live show?
A: Yes. The studio produces AI-generated content on local and cloud pipelines and prepares it for the real screen or surface like any other content, at the right resolution and format. Zori uses AI every day, including AI coding agents that automate parts of the pipeline, such as Unreal scripting, rendering and encoding.

Q: Can you make seamless loops that a venue plays every day?
A: Yes. The VIP rooms DepthLab designed run seamless loops daily in Resolume Arena. Venue staff choose them, and no operator is needed.

Q: What should I send to start a content project?
A: Send the screen or projector layout with resolutions, photos or plans of the space, where people watch from, the theme or references you have in mind, and the date it must be ready. If the setup is not planned yet, the studio can plan it together with the content.

Q: How much does custom content cost?
A: DepthLab does not publish prices. The cost depends on the number and length of the pieces, the size of the canvas, the amount of 3D or AI work, and how many versions the space needs.

## Real-Time AI
URL: https://depth-lab.com/ai/

DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, develops real-time AI installations for entertainment venues, malls and museums in Israel, starting with a real-time AI mirror. You stand in front of a camera and see yourself in another world: live AI video made from the camera image, running locally on one GPU, now at about 10 FPS. The mirror is still in R&D, and AI is also part of the studio's everyday content pipeline.

- Real-time AI mirror R&D: a camera, one local GPU, and you in another world
- AI installation concepts for entertainment venues, malls and museums
- Pipeline optimization and custom LoRA training
- AI-generated content for screens, rooms and shows
- AI coding agents that automate parts of the pipeline: Unreal scripting, rendering and encoding

### The real-time AI mirror: live AI video from a camera
A client asked for a real-time AI mirror: you stand in front of a camera and see yourself in another world, with everything running locally on one GPU. The deal did not close. The project had become interesting, so Zori kept working on it.

### What the R&D clips show
In the R&D clips, a man stands in an ordinary living room, and in the AI image the floor around him has turned into sand and shallow surf. He crouches to put his hands in the water and kicks at the small waves, and the AI image moves with him. Before-and-after clips show the camera image next to the same moment after the AI.

### From about 5 to about 10 FPS
The hard part is speed. Video AI models render clips in minutes, and a mirror needs several new frames every second. The first version ran at about 5 FPS. After optimizing the pipeline and training his own LoRA, Zori reached about 10 FPS on the same GPU. The work is still in progress.

### AI installations for venues, malls and museums
Zori sees the mirror as an AI installation for entertainment venues, malls and museums. Visitors become part of the content: each person who steps in front of the camera sees a live image of themselves in another world.

### AI in the content pipeline
Zori uses AI every day. The studio produces AI-generated content on local and cloud pipelines, and uses AI coding agents to automate parts of the pipeline, such as Unreal scripting, rendering and encoding.

1. Concept: We define what visitors do and what they see, for the specific space and audience.
2. Local prototype: A test on one local GPU shows the real speed and look early.
3. Tuning: The pipeline is optimized and, where it helps, a custom LoRA is trained.
4. Installation: Camera, screen or projection and the computer are set up in the space and tested with visitors.

Q: Is there a real-time AI mirror installation in Israel?
A: DepthLab, the Tel Aviv studio of Zori Baazov, is developing one. In the R&D version you stand in front of a camera and see yourself in another world, running locally on one GPU at about 10 FPS. The work is still in progress.

Q: What is real-time AI video, and why is it hard?
A: Real-time AI video, also called live AI video, is video in which an AI model changes the live camera image as it happens, for example turning a living room floor into sand and sea around the person standing in it. The hard part is speed: video AI models usually render clips in minutes, and a live installation needs several new frames every second. The DepthLab mirror reaches about 10 FPS on one local GPU.

Q: Can AI video run in real time on one local GPU?
A: Yes, at a limited frame rate. The first version of the DepthLab mirror ran at about 5 FPS. After optimizing the pipeline and training his own LoRA, Zori reached about 10 FPS on the same GPU.

Q: What is the difference between an AI mirror and an AI photo booth?
A: An AI photo booth takes a picture and returns an edited image after a short wait. A real-time AI mirror shows a live, moving image, so you see yourself in another world while you move. That needs several new frames every second, which makes it much harder to build.

Q: Can I book the AI mirror for an event?
A: The real-time AI mirror is still in R&D. DepthLab is developing it as an AI installation for entertainment venues, malls and museums. To ask about it for a space or an event, send a DM on Instagram or a message on LinkedIn with the place and the date.

Q: Who can build an AI installation for a mall, a museum or an entertainment venue in Israel?
A: DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, is developing real-time AI installations for these spaces, starting with the AI mirror R&D. The studio also plans and builds the rest of such a piece: cameras and sensors, screens or projection, content and installation.

Q: Why train a custom LoRA?
A: A LoRA is a small add-on trained on top of an AI model to teach it a specific look or behavior. In the mirror R&D, training his own LoRA was part of the work that took the speed from about 5 FPS to about 10 FPS on the same GPU.

Q: How does DepthLab use AI in content production?
A: Zori uses AI every day. The studio produces AI-generated content on local and cloud pipelines, and AI coding agents automate parts of the pipeline, such as Unreal scripting, rendering and encoding.

## Custom projects

These aren't all the services. For much more, like custom AI agents, building control systems, permanent installations and space design, you're welcome to get in touch too.

## Live 3D LED Tower
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/led-tower-live/
 · 2026 · Zori Baazov (DepthLab): pixel mapping, LED looks and live operation

A 2.5 m LED tower of four LED modules, about 20,400 pixels, that Zori played live from his TouchDesigner deck. Each module was placed in 3D the way it really stood and checked pixel by pixel, so shapes like a ball or rising fire move through the whole volume, not across a flat screen.

- Type: 3D LED installation, played live
- Size: Four LED modules, 0.5 × 0.5 m each and 2.5 m tall, standing as one tower
- Pixels: About 20,400 (5,100 per module)
- Control: TouchDesigner and Art-Net, one controller per module
- Role: Zori Baazov (DepthLab): pixel mapping, LED looks and live operation

### The tower
Four LED modules stand together as one tower, 2.5 m tall. Every LED has a fixed place in 3D, so a look is drawn into the volume: a ball can float inside it and fire can rise through it.

### From the preview to the real LEDs
On site, a mapping tool placed every module in 3D the way it really stood, sent test patterns to check every row and pixel, and handed the map to TouchDesigner. The ball seen in the tool's 3D preview then appeared on the real LEDs.

### Live
Zori ran the looks live from his TouchDesigner deck, with each module on its own Art-Net controller.

## LED DJ Stage, Designed in Unreal Engine
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/led-dj-stage-concept/
Stage concept (simulation), Tel Aviv · 2026 · Zori Baazov (DepthLab): stage design, LED looks, light cues and rendering

A DJ stage of LED cubes, the same model as Zori's real LED modules, built as a simulation in Unreal Engine with every LED in place. Zori plays his deck's looks on it, keys the club lights (beams, strobes and blinders) to the same music and renders the show, so a producer can see the stage, the content and the lights together before anything is built. The stage itself doesn't exist yet.

- Type: LED stage concept, simulated and rendered
- Stage: Nine LED cubes around the DJ, and other layouts: a horizon line, an arch, a ring and a gate with a screen
- Tools: Unreal Engine, TouchDesigner, Art-Net and DMX, Movie Render Queue
- Status: Concept: the stage exists as a simulation
- Role: Zori Baazov (DepthLab): stage design, LED looks, light cues and rendering

### Layouts
The cubes stand around the DJ in different layouts: a ring, a horizon line, an arch or a gate with a screen, each with its own looks. The cube model is the same as Zori's real LED modules, so every look is made for real hardware.

### Content and light together
The LED looks and the club lights follow one score measured to the music, so drops, cuts to black and light hits land together in the render.

### Before the build
The stage exists as a simulation and rendered video, ready for a producer or a venue that wants to build it.

## LAB: Experiments
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/lab-video-mapping/
 · 2026 · Zori Baazov (DepthLab): experiments and prototypes

LAB is where Zori runs his experiments, and then tries to bring them into the real world: LEDs that follow his hand, live closed-circuit cameras, real-time AI, generative visuals and video mapping on real objects. Some have already reached the stage, like the moon and the carved log at Omri Smadar's party.

- Type: Experiments: LEDs, hand control, closed-circuit cameras, real-time AI, generative visuals, video mapping
- Tools: TouchDesigner, GLSL and software written with AI coding agents
- Status: In development

### Hand control
While the LED cube was being built at home, a sphere of light inside the hanging LEDs followed a hand up and down. On a building facade, the projected light followed a raised arm.

### Closed circuit
Live camera feeds become the material: the picture from closed-circuit cameras is glitched and rewound in real time and shown on a giant screen above the DJ booth.

### Real-time AI
In real-time AI tests, a living room turns into a space station, and the person walking through it into an astronaut.

### Generative visuals
Looks from Zori's TouchDesigner deck, like a black disc with a corona of light filaments around it, are tried here first.

### Video mapping on objects
On a carved relief at the studio, the looks grow out of the relief's own rings and edges. A projector throws patterns of light and a camera reads them, so every object gets a measured mask and depth that go straight into TouchDesigner.

### From LAB to the real world
The experiments go out into shows and installations: the inflatable moon and the carved wooden log at Omri Smadar's party, the LED tower that was first seen in a 3D preview and then played live, and the LED cube at Midburn.

## Omri Smadar's Party: Stage Design and Video Mapping
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/audio-reactive-stage-mapping/
Omri Smadar's party · 2025-2026 · Zori Baazov (DepthLab): stage design, video mapping and visuals

For Omri Smadar's party, DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, designed the stage and made custom video mapping for it: an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log on stage, mapped with real-time generative looks, together with Erez Cohen. Earlier, for Omri Smadar's live shows, Zori Baazov made audio-reactive visuals for each song with a live closed-circuit camera.

- Type: Stage design, video mapping and show visuals
- Role: Zori Baazov (DepthLab): stage design, video mapping and visuals
- Party: Stage design and custom video mapping on an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log, with real-time generative looks
- Live shows: Audio-reactive visuals made for each song, with a live closed-circuit camera
- With: Stage video mapping together with Erez Cohen
- Runtime: Real time, during the party and the shows

### Stage design and video mapping
For Omri Smadar's party, DepthLab designed the stage and made custom video mapping for it. The video was mapped onto two objects on the stage, an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log. The looks on them were generative and ran in real time during the party. The stage mapping was made together with Erez Cohen.

### Visuals for each song
Earlier, for Omri Smadar's live shows, each song had its own visuals, made to react to the audio as the song is played. A live closed-circuit camera was part of the setup.

### How it works
Mapping onto objects starts from their real shape, so the content sits on the object itself rather than on a flat screen. Audio-reactive visuals take their movement from the sound, so the image follows the song as it is played.

### For musicians and event producers
A project like this combines stage design with two DepthLab services: video mapping on the stage set, and live visuals that respond to the music. The stage, the objects on it and the visuals then come together as one audiovisual show.

## Immersive VIP Room Design
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/immersive-vip-rooms/
Entertainment venue, three VIP rooms · 2026 · Content, mapping and playback system

DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, designed three immersive VIP rooms at an entertainment venue. Each room wraps the viewer in projection on three walls, about 270 degrees, and two of the rooms can open into one picture. Sixteen visuals run there every day as seamless loops, built and rendered mostly in Unreal Engine to the real wall sizes, the projector layout and the resolution of the rooms. The venue staff choose them with no operator.

- Type: Immersive room design: permanent projection rooms
- Role: Zori Baazov (DepthLab): content, mapping and playback system
- System: Five to six projectors per room on three walls, about 270 degrees; one 5120 x 800 px canvas per room; two rooms can open into one continuous image
- Runtime: Sixteen visuals as seamless loops, every day; venue staff choose them, no operator
- Tools: Unreal Engine, Resolume Arena

### Made for the real walls
Each room has five to six projectors, blended into one image across the three walls. The visuals are made to the real wall sizes, the projector layout and the resolution. The worlds were built mostly in Unreal Engine, with a camera rig matched to the measured walls, and every visual is rendered as one wide canvas of 5120 x 800 px per room and adapted to the geometry and viewing position of that room.

### The worlds
The content is sixteen visuals, more than a dozen themed worlds for kids, teens and adults: among them a magic forest, a jungle and an ice world for kids; open space, a spaceship cockpit and a space station for ages 9 to 14; and a mansion, a casino, a city at sunset and a city in the sky for adults. The gallery shows the rooms during the installation, and the worlds as full rendered canvases.

### Zori's role and daily playback
Zori Baazov of DepthLab made the content, mapped it to the rooms and set up the playback system. Seamless loops now run there daily in Resolume Arena as the permanent runtime. The venue staff choose which world plays, and no operator is needed.

## Real-Time AI Mirror
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/real-time-ai-mirror/
In-house R&D · 2026 · R&D: real-time pipeline and custom LoRA training

DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, is developing a real-time AI mirror for entertainment venues, malls and museums: you stand in front of a camera and see yourself in another world, with everything running locally on one GPU. The first version ran at about 5 FPS; after optimizing the pipeline and training his own LoRA, Zori Baazov reached about 10 FPS on the same GPU. The project is still in R&D.

- Type: Real-time AI installation, R&D
- Role: Zori Baazov (DepthLab): real-time pipeline and custom LoRA training
- System: A live camera and one local GPU; a custom LoRA trained in-house
- Runtime: Real time: about 5 FPS in the first version, about 10 FPS on the same GPU after optimization

### The brief
A client asked for a real-time AI mirror on one local GPU. The deal did not close, but the project had become interesting, so Zori kept working on it as in-house R&D.

### How it works
The live camera image goes through an AI model on one local GPU, and the visitor sees the same moment in another world. The hard part is speed: video AI models render clips in minutes, and a mirror needs several new frames every second.

### Zori's role and where it is going
Zori builds the real-time pipeline and trains the custom LoRA. He sees the mirror as an AI installation for entertainment venues, malls and museums, where each visitor in front of the camera sees a live image of themselves in another world.

### What the gallery shows
Side by side, the camera image shows a man in an ordinary living room, and the AI version shows the same moment with the floor turned into a beach. In the clips he stands in shallow surf with his arms out, kicks at small waves and crouches to touch the water.

## Daskal Live Show: Timecode Visuals
URL: https://depth-lab.com/work/daskal-live-show/
Live shows · 2025, ongoing · Visual show design, timecode and live operation

Zori Baazov of DepthLab, a Tel Aviv studio, built a timecode-based visual show for Daskal, a keyboardist, composer and producer, so his live set plays as one audiovisual show. The show has a visual language built for the set, content synced to the music via timecode and a cue list. Zori runs it live at every show.

- Type: Audiovisual live show, timecode-based
- Role: Zori Baazov (DepthLab): visual show design, timecode and live operation
- Show: Music: Daskal, keyboardist, composer and producer. Visuals: a visual language built for the set, synced via timecode, with a cue list
- Runtime: Live, operated by Zori at every date

### The show
The show is built for Daskal's live set and has a visual language of its own. In the gallery, line drawings, clouds, blossom-like textures and dotted patterns move across the wall behind his keyboards, with spiral patterns on the LED columns above.

### How it works
The content is locked to the music by timecode, a shared time signal, so each cue lands at the same moment in the music at every show. The cue points of the set are organized in a cue list.

### Zori's role
The music is Daskal's, and the visual show is Zori's: he designed it, set up the timecode sync and the cue list, and operates it live at every date.

## Zori Baazov, VJ & Real-Time Experience Creator in Tel Aviv
Zori Baazov (זורי באזוב), a VJ and visual artist based in Tel Aviv, makes audiovisual shows for musicians and live visuals for clubs and festivals across Israel. He founded DepthLab (Depth Lab Studio), a studio for live visuals, projection mapping and interactive installations, from stage shows to permanent rooms.
Zori was born in Georgia and moved to Israel. He studied New Media at Musrara, the Naggar School of Art and Society, in Jerusalem: creative coding, video and sensor-based installations.
He started as a VJ in clubs, at parties and fashion shows. Later he worked as a VJ and real-time operator on large concert productions: LED screens, projection, on-stage troubleshooting, and working with directors, lighting designers and artists.
Since founding DepthLab, he has worked directly with clients, taking projects from site survey to handover: specification, system design (projectors, LED, media servers, sensors), suppliers and budget, content, installation and calibration.
On stage he mostly works with electronic music. He wants the visuals to follow the arrangement of a set, its drops and breakdowns, and to react to the frequencies as well.
For Daskal, a keyboardist, composer and producer, he built a timecode show that turns the live set into one audiovisual show, and he runs it live at every show. For Omri Smadar's live shows he made audio-reactive visuals for each song with a live closed-circuit camera. For Omri Smadar's party he designed the stage and mapped video with real-time generative scenes onto an inflatable moon and a carved wooden log.
He uses AI every day, including AI coding agents that automate parts of his pipeline, such as Unreal scripting, rendering and encoding. His R&D includes a real-time AI mirror. In development: an immersive rehabilitation room for a hospital's clinical team, with markerless body tracking on depth cameras.
DepthLab is open to studio projects for entertainment venues, malls, museums, events and brands across Israel. Zori is also open to roles in real-time and interactive experiences, live production and multimedia project management.

Selected venues and events:
- White Night, Tel Aviv Museum of Art
- Hasifa Music Festival
- Midburn
- Midbari
- Oman 17

Talks and appearances:
